messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 45
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Military Medic
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 66

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Threat: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
  Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Confused Sequence: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore, Identity Loss: I feel like I don't know myself anymore, Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Daniel Kraus was 45, a widowed military medic from a German-American family, and when he first came to treatment he spoke with the flattened precision of someone used to staying functional under pressure. The flood had struck the town where his unit had been deployed during a major disaster response, and he still described the night in fragments: the siren cutting out, the generator failing, water pushing through the streets, people shouting from dark windows, a child separated from her mother in the chaos. He had been moving from one trapped resident to another with his pack and stretcher when a collapsing wall sent a shock through the building and pinned part of the stairwell. In the months that followed, Daniel found that any sudden bang—a dropped tray in the supermarket, a backfiring engine outside his apartment, even a door slamming in the clinic—sent him instantly into high alert. At work in the military medical unit he watched every corridor and doorway, sat where he could see exits, and never quite let himself relax, even in places everyone else treated as safe.

The memory of the flood did not return to him as a tidy story. When it came, it came as terror, as if his body had been dropped back into the same night; he would stop mid-sentence, stare, and need time before he could continue. He said the scenes would not stay in order: the faces, the waterline, the shouting, the trapped stairwell, and the moment he realized he could not get to everyone. That confusion made the memory feel even more unbearable, and the more it overwhelmed him, the more he came to believe that something in him had broken beyond repair. He had once defined himself by being calm under fire, by knowing what to do when others panicked, and now he felt he no longer knew who he was. He told the clinician that nothing in his life felt meaningful anymore, that the beliefs he had once lived by—that competence mattered, that suffering could be organized into service, that the world could still be made orderly through training and duty—had been shattered by what he had seen in the flood.

Those same beliefs about himself and the world then colored the memories when they arrived again. If the images rushed back while he was alone, he would think, with a grim certainty, that he had failed the people he was supposed to protect, and that he had become someone unrecognizable to himself. What had happened in the disaster seemed, in his mind, to prove that his old understanding of the world was false, and the memory became easier to summon in its emotional weight than in any coherent sequence. He would begin to replay the scene, not to make sense of it but to test where he had gone wrong, and each attempt left him more convinced that there was no stable meaning left to hold onto. The result was a narrowing of his life: he avoided news about storms, declined invitations that would take him near water, and kept himself busy with extra shifts because idleness made the recollections more likely to break through. At home, in the quiet apartment he now inhabited alone, the silence had become as hard to bear as the memories, and he would leave the television on just to cover the spaces in which his mind might drift back.

The body of the fear never fully stood down. Daniel remained keyed to sudden sound, scanning before he entered rooms, stiffening whenever footsteps echoed in the hallway outside his quarters. He knew, intellectually, that he was not back in the flood, but his body did not behave as if it believed him. The watchfulness fed his sense that the world was no longer trustworthy, and that conviction made it harder to settle when the memory returned, because each recall seemed to confirm that nothing had been restored. He spoke of going to sleep already braced for an alarm, of feeling unable to relax even after long, uneventful days, and of hating how quickly he now measured every environment for danger. As his fear of sounds and his constant guarding continued, he found himself more alone, more withdrawn from colleagues and friends, and more certain that the man his wife had known was gone. He had finally sought help after catching himself freezing in the medic station when a metal cart crashed in the corridor, his chest tight and his mind flooded with the flood again. What he most feared was that this was the rest of his life: that the terror, the disordered memories, and the sense of having lost both his purpose and his identity would never let him return to himself.
